This civilian shift to advanced energy technologies will impact DOW missions in several ways in the next 10– 20 years. DOW, well known as the largest single energy consumer in the U.S. federal government (U.S. CRS 2019), will most likely be competing with the civilian sector for energy supplies. Moreover, the demand for energy, both in military and non-military sectors, is projected to increase in the next 25 years (EIA 2023). U.S. electricity demand is estimated to increase by almost 16% by 2029 (Wilson, Zimmerman, and Gramlich 2024) and 78% by 2050 from 2023 levels (Batra et al. 2025), in part due to the rapid increase in demand driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers. For example, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE)-funded analysis projects a compound annual growth rate in data center electricity consumption of 13% to 27% between 2023 and 2028 (Shehabi et al. 2024). Military energy use has increased from approximately 1 gallon of fuel per soldier per day during World War II, to approximately 4 gallons during the 1990–1991 Persian Gulf War, to 16 gallons by 2006 in Iraq and Afghanistan (Crowley et al. 2007), and 22 gallons in 2011 (ASA IE&E 2011). Future demand is expected to grow as DOW adopts energy-intensive technologies such as AI, employs more dispersed operational strategies, and develops directed energy weapons (Jafari et al. 2024; Simulcik, Villalobos, and Bazilian 2025). Meeting this surging demand while ensuring energy security and resilience will likely depend on the timely expansion and deployment of energy generation and storage technologies. Without proactive efforts, both military and civilian sectors risk facing energy shortfalls. Like any large-scale change, the adoption of advanced energy technologies introduces new risks. Many of these risks are mitigated during normal operations but could become more challenging during conflicts or large-scale combat operations. Mapping interconnected risks and identifying mitigation strategies should help position DOW to reduce these risks and chart a path forward. 1 Advanced energy technologies addressed in this report include batteries/energy storage, photovoltaics, wind, geothermal, synthetic aviation fuels, hydrogen, and marine/hydrokinetic power. 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 Drivers of Infrastructure Risk As countries around the world adopt advanced energy technologies to increase energy production and enhance resilience, adopters must consider risks to new infrastructure. Risks to and from electricity infrastructure have always existed, and advanced energy technologies can amplify some vulnerabilities and introduce novel risks. 2.1 Expanded Electrification The increasing electrification of assets from vehicles to building heating systems is happening around the globe at varying rates, potentially exacerbating existing vulnerabilities, such as a dependence on local grids, including in overseas locations.
